variants.name: Non-blocking Fiber with a Fiber::Scheduler
variants.implementation_notes: Ruby gives the machinery but not the completion carrier, so the classic structure is hand-written: the token is the fiber that must be resumed (or the Proc the service is asked to call), and the demultiplexing loop is a Fiber::Scheduler implementation that resumes the waiting fiber when its I/O is ready. Because Ruby's fibers are cooperative and never preempted, ownership and dispatch stay a programmer decision - the same 'manual' position as C, where the language supplies the primitives and the token discipline is yours. Frameworks move the loop out of the application: EventMachine::Deferrable (callback/errback) is the historic version, the async gem's fiber-scheduler tasks the modern one.
variants.code_sketch:
Fiber.set_scheduler(MyScheduler.new)        # resumes fibers when their I/O is ready
task = Fiber.schedule do                   # the fiber + its yield point are the token
  reply = service.call(request)            # yields; the scheduler resumes this fiber
  handle(reply)
end
pitfalls: Fibers are cooperative and never preempted: without Fiber.set_scheduler a non-blocking fiber behaves exactly like a blocking one, and Fiber.schedule raises RuntimeError('No scheduler is available!').
A Fiber handle is a single-use token - resuming a terminated fiber raises FiberError('dead fiber called'), and raising into a fiber owned by another thread also raises FiberError.
A Proc token retains its closure: if the service never calls it, the request state stays reachable, so keep an explicit registry with timeouts rather than waiting for the garbage collector.

variants.name: Thread::Queue completion channel
variants.implementation_notes: Queued completion notifications in core Ruby: completing threads push the request's handler together with its payload onto a Thread::Queue, and one demux thread blocks in pop and runs whatever comes back - the pushed proc is the token, the queue is the completion channel, and no table keyed on request identity is consulted. This is the shape to use when completions arrive from other threads (or from a pool) and the client wants to control when it processes them; it is also the only form that works without a scheduler.
variants.code_sketch:
completions = Thread::Queue.new                 # queued completion notifications
service.register(request) { |reply| completions.push([request.handler, reply]) }
loop do
  handler, reply = completions.pop              # the pushed token demuxes it
  break if reply == :shutdown
  handler.call(reply)
end
pitfalls: Thread::Queue#pop blocks when the queue is empty (deq(true) raises ThreadError), pushing to a closed queue raises ClosedQueueError, and an unbounded queue grows forever if the demux loop lags.
The handler pushed with the payload is still the token: if the producer pushes a handler for a request the consumer already abandoned, the state it closes over must already have been released.
